results.name: presentation_order_forward_bias
results.description: On 2+ example sets, (yes above max minus yes below min) for sets shown in ascending order minus the same for sets shown in descending order; observed above null means the upward lean follows the direction the examples were shown in (which the order-blind model misses), below null means descending order strengthens it.
results.code:
# name: presentation_order_forward_bias
# description: On 2+ example sets, (yes above max minus yes below min) for sets shown in ascending order minus the same for sets shown in descending order; observed above null means the upward lean follows the direction the examples were shown in (which the order-blind model misses), below null means descending order strengthens it.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values.astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    n = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(1)
    mx = np.nanmax(ex, 1); mn = np.nanmin(ex, 1)
    isex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(1)
    k = ex.shape[1]
    d = np.diff(ex, axis=1)
    valid = ~np.isnan(d)
    asc = (n >= 2) & np.where(valid, d > 0, True).all(1)
    desc = (n >= 2) & np.where(valid, d < 0, True).all(1)
    up = (t > mx) & ~isex; dn = (t < mn) & ~isex
    def gap(m):
        a = r[m & up]; b = r[m & dn]
        if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
            return 0.0
        return a.mean() - b.mean()
    return float(gap(asc) - gap(desc))

results.name: above_max_distance_decay
results.description: On 2+ example sets, yes rate for non-example targets 1-10 above the largest example minus targets more than 20 above it; observed above null means the forward lean is local continuation that decays with distance (the model's lean is flat), below null means far upward targets are accepted more than predicted.
results.code:
# name: above_max_distance_decay
# description: On 2+ example sets, yes rate for non-example targets 1-10 above the largest example minus targets more than 20 above it; observed above null means the forward lean is local continuation that decays with distance (the model's lean is flat), below null means far upward targets are accepted more than predicted.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values.astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    n = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(1)
    mx = np.nanmax(ex, 1); mn = np.nanmin(ex, 1)
    isex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(1)
    m = (n >= 2) & ~isex
    gap = t - mx
    a = r[m & (gap >= 1) & (gap <= 10)]; b = r[m & (gap > 20)]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: span_center_vs_edge_gap
results.description: On 3-4 example sets with span at least 20, among non-example targets strictly inside the span, yes rate for targets in the middle 40% of the span minus those in the outer 20% at each end; observed above null means people treat the span centre as more typical than the model's flat interval hypotheses, below null means edges near examples are favoured.
results.code:
# name: span_center_vs_edge_gap
# description: On 3-4 example sets with span at least 20, among non-example targets strictly inside the span, yes rate for targets in the middle 40% of the span minus those in the outer 20% at each end; observed above null means people treat the span centre as more typical than the model's flat interval hypotheses, below null means edges near examples are favoured.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values.astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    n = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(1)
    mx = np.nanmax(ex, 1); mn = np.nanmin(ex, 1)
    isex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(1)
    span = mx - mn
    pos = (t - mn) / np.where(span > 0, span, 1)
    m = (n >= 3) & (span >= 20) & ~isex & (t > mn) & (t < mx)
    a = r[m & (pos >= 0.3) & (pos <= 0.7)]; b = r[m & ((pos < 0.2) | (pos > 0.8))]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: digit_reversal_target_yes_gap
results.description: Yes rate for non-example two-digit targets that are the digit reversal of some example (e.g. 27 after 72, excluding palindromes) minus other non-example targets on sets with at least one non-palindromic two-digit example; observed above null means people accept digit-reversed numbers beyond what the model's concepts imply, below null means they reject them more.
results.code:
# name: digit_reversal_target_yes_gap
# description: Yes rate for non-example two-digit targets that are the digit reversal of some example (e.g. 27 after 72, excluding palindromes) minus other non-example targets on sets with at least one non-palindromic two-digit example; observed above null means people accept digit-reversed numbers beyond what the model's concepts imply, below null means they reject them more.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values.astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    n = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(1)
    mx = np.nanmax(ex, 1); mn = np.nanmin(ex, 1)
    isex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(1)
    e = np.nan_to_num(ex, nan=-1).astype(int)
    two = (e >= 10) & (e <= 99) & (e % 10 != e // 10) & (e % 10 != 0)
    rev = np.where(two, (e % 10) * 10 + e // 10, -999)
    hit = (rev == t[:, None]).any(1) & ~isex
    elig = two.any(1) & ~isex
    a = r[hit]; b = r[elig & ~hit]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: even_set_parity_gap
results.description: On 2+ example sets whose examples are all even, yes rate for even non-example targets minus odd non-example targets; observed above null means people generalise 'even' more sharply than the model, below null means they ignore shared evenness more than predicted.
results.code:
# name: even_set_parity_gap
# description: On 2+ example sets whose examples are all even, yes rate for even non-example targets minus odd non-example targets; observed above null means people generalise 'even' more sharply than the model, below null means they ignore shared evenness more than predicted.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values.astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    n = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(1)
    mx = np.nanmax(ex, 1); mn = np.nanmin(ex, 1)
    isex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(1)
    e = np.nan_to_num(ex, nan=2)
    alleven = (n >= 2) & (e % 2 == 0).all(1)
    m = alleven & ~isex
    a = r[m & (t % 2 == 0)]; b = r[m & (t % 2 == 1)]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: arithmetic_next_term_yes_gap
results.description: On 2+ example sets, yes rate for the target equal to last shown example plus (last minus second-to-last) minus yes rate for other non-example targets of the same sets; observed above null means people extrapolate the shown sequence's step more than the concept model predicts, below null means less.
results.code:
# name: arithmetic_next_term_yes_gap
# description: On 2+ example sets, yes rate for the target equal to last shown example plus (last minus second-to-last) minus yes rate for other non-example targets of the same sets; observed above null means people extrapolate the shown sequence's step more than the concept model predicts, below null means less.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values.astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    n = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(1)
    mx = np.nanmax(ex, 1); mn = np.nanmin(ex, 1)
    isex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(1)
    rows = np.arange(len(t))
    li = np.clip(n - 1, 0, None); pi = np.clip(n - 2, 0, None)
    last = ex[rows, li]; prev = ex[rows, pi]
    nxt = 2 * last - prev
    m = (n >= 2) & ~isex
    hit = m & (t == nxt) & (last != prev)
    a = r[hit]; b = r[m & ~hit]
    if len(a) == 0 or len(b) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(a.mean() - b.mean())

results.name: same_set_lag1_response_agreement
results.description: Among consecutive trials (trial_index increasing by 1) with the same number_set, fraction where the response repeats the previous response; observed above null means response perseveration/sequential dependence the independent-trial model lacks, below null means alternation.
results.code:
# name: same_set_lag1_response_agreement
# description: Among consecutive trials (trial_index increasing by 1) with the same number_set, fraction where the response repeats the previous response; observed above null means response perseveration/sequential dependence the independent-trial model lacks, below null means alternation.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values.astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    n = (~np.isnan(ex)).sum(1)
    mx = np.nanmax(ex, 1); mn = np.nanmin(ex, 1)
    isex = (ex == t[:, None]).any(1)
    ti = df["trial_index"].astype(int).values
    s = df["number_set"].astype(str).values
    if len(r) < 2:
        return 0.0
    same = (s[1:] == s[:-1]) & (ti[1:] == ti[:-1] + 1)
    if same.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float((r[1:] == r[:-1])[same].mean())
